column3: The preceding summons about claimed partners frames the same Day of questioning and exposes false claims before the question about messengers.
Noah's answered call provides a contrast between divine response and the human response demanded in the focus ayah.
It identifies the addressee as a messenger but adds little beyond the focus ayah's explicit mention of messengers.
The repeated partner-question confirms the recurring court setting, though its wording is already supplied by 28:62.
The failed response of claimed partners and the sight of punishment directly set up the reversal to asking what was answered to the messengers.
Responding to God and the messenger after injury supplies a concrete positive form of the response under examination.
It gives the closest parallel: God gathers the messengers and asks what response they received.
Noah's call receiving an answer contrasts a fulfilled call with the accountability for answering messengers.
God's answer to believers' prayer is a different direction of response from the collective answer sought in the focus ayah.
A Day-of-Gathering inquiry into who misled worshippers supplies a close judicial counterpart to the focus question.
The disavowal of those who led others astray is an immediate part of the same court scene and clarifies responsibility.
Noah's public warning establishes the messenger's prior address to a people later accountable for their reply.
The commanded call to alleged partners receives no answer, closely contrasting the required answer to the messengers.
The reports becoming inaccessible directly continues the focus question by showing why further reciprocal questioning ceases.
Sending the she-camel as a test does not materially clarify the answer given to messengers.
Lot's identity as a messenger adds only a general instance of the messenger category.
Its reciprocal questioning about the great report provides a limited echo of the silenced questioning in the surrounding scene.
Messengers bring clear proofs to their peoples before punishment, supplying the warning-and-accountability sequence.
The denial of messengers gives a concise negative answer pattern relevant to the focus question.
Moses and Aaron's declaration of mission establishes a messenger scene without showing the people's response.
A people reject several sent messengers, giving a direct instance of the response being assessed.
A general blessing on messengers does not add to the focus ayah's inquiry into their reception.
The demand that each community produce proof is the immediate next phase of the same judgment setting.
Believers responding to their Lord gives a constructive communal counterpart to answering the messengers.
Its Day-of-judgment call about claimed partners closely parallels the court formula, though earlier cards already establish it.
The leaders' denial of coercive authority locates responsibility with the transgressing people, relevant to their answer.
God's answer to a plea for aid is only an inverse and individual form of response.
Thamud's denial of messengers is another direct negative response, but it adds little after earlier denial examples.
The angels' annunciation to Mary is not an account of a community answering messengers.
The universal mercy of the Prophet's sending supplies only broad mission context.
When asked what their Lord sent down, the deniers dismiss it as old tales, a pertinent refusal of revealed address.
Noah's rescue follows the call narrative but does not itself concern a response to messengers.
The sending of devils to incite disbelievers is a different use of sending and does not clarify the court question.
Wrongdoers promise too late to answer God's call and follow the messengers, directly showing the answer sought in the focus ayah.
The drowning of Noah's deniers shows the consequence of rejecting divine signs after the messenger's call.
Peoples reject clear human messengers because of their humanity, directly specifying one answer for which they are accountable.
The question about the purpose of a parable is not an answer to the messengers themselves.
The angels' call to Zachariah is unrelated to the collective judgment of messenger response.
Opposition to God and His messenger gives a broad hostile stance without an answer scene.
The God-fearing answer that their Lord sent good forms a positive counterpart to 16:24's dismissive reply.
The request to release Israel concerns political departure rather than answering a messenger's message.
God's answer to Joseph's prayer is an inverse response and has limited bearing on the focus inquiry.
A legal question addressed to the Prophet does not add to the accountability for answering messengers.
Deniers will receive the reports they mocked, supporting the focus scene's eventual exposure of rejected messages.
Lot's people answer his rebuke by demanding punishment, a concrete defiant reply to a messenger.
Asking visiting messengers their business supplies only a surface mention of messengers.
The blindness contrast loosely echoes the following loss of reports but does not address messenger response.
Believers respond and act righteously, offering a positive answer pattern distinct from the condemned response.
This repeats the question to visiting messengers without illuminating how a people answered them.
God's call commissioning Moses toward the wrongdoing people establishes the mission whose response becomes accountable.
Elijah's identity as a messenger is generic context with no reception or answer.
The wrongdoer's regret at not taking a way with the messenger portrays the consequence of a failed response.
The command to stop them because they will be questioned closely supports the interrogative judgment setting.
The Prophet's roles as witness, bearer of good news, and warner explain why a response to a messenger bears consequence.
The devil's oath is not a response to a messenger.
Assurance that God hears Moses and Aaron during their mission provides only indirect mission context.
Mutual response between God and worshippers offers a theological contrast to refusing a messenger's call.
Satan's threat to obstruct the straight path does not clarify the answer to messengers.
Moses' request to send for Aaron concerns delivery capacity, not the audience's response.
Jonah's identity as a messenger adds no specific account of reception.
On the Day God calls, people respond, giving a direct eschatological response scene parallel to the focus ayah.
The naming and protection of Mary is unrelated to answering messengers.
The affirmation that Muhammad is among the messengers is general and redundant mission context.
The command to listen for the caller's near Day-of-judgment summons closely frames the focus ayah's call.
Mutual accusation in judgment provides a related pattern of people answering one another under scrutiny.
Moses brings truth and clear proof before demanding Israel's release, giving a substantive messenger address.
The recipient's public reading of his record is an accountability image but not a response to messengers.
The warning that they will know is too general to add to the focus question.
Hostility toward God's messengers identifies rejection but does not depict the answer or its judgment scene.
Claimed partners neither hear nor respond and will deny the association on Resurrection, sharply clarifying false calls beside the messenger question.
This repeats the earlier warning without additional relevance.
Lot's people answer his reforming call by expelling his household, a concrete corrupt response to a messenger.
The arrival of Lot's messengers creates narrative context but no answer from the addressed people.
The great report loosely relates to the lost reports after the focus ayah but adds no clear response link.
The messenger's role as bearer of news and warning, without responsibility for the Fire's people, clarifies the limits of messenger accountability.
The people of al-Hijr explicitly deny the messengers, a direct negative answer to the focus question.
The Prophet confirms the messengers with truth, supplying a positive counterpart to their rejection.
Pharaoh's dispatch of gatherers is a different, coercive use of sending.
God states that He will question both those sent to and the messengers, directly matching the focus ayah's accountability structure.
The reciprocal questioning of the condemned provides a related judgment-scene interaction.
A messenger is sent as a witness, explaining why the response of recipients can be examined.
Misreading restricted provision as humiliation does not address messengers or their reception.
The condemned acknowledge the Lord's word and impending punishment, a related judicial admission.
Failure to answer a challenge is a different kind of response and does not concern messengers' reception.
The question about a missing item is unrelated to the focus ayah.
The command to call on God and the warning against pride offer a broader contrast between response and arrogant refusal.
Thamud defy Salih's command and demand the promised punishment if he is a messenger, an explicit hostile answer.
Noah is sent to warn his people before painful punishment, establishing the prior mission behind later accountability.
Messengers bring good news and warning before belief or reform determines the outcome, clarifying the purpose of their address.
The people deny their own messenger despite knowing him, giving a specific form of refusal.
The splitting sky and descending angels supply only broad Day-of-judgment background.
The messenger must convey, not control acceptance, clarifying why recipients themselves answer for their response.
A Day-of-gathering address to human and jinn allies supplies a related court scene of associations and final liability.
Distribution of property through the messenger does not materially concern answering messengers.
Abraham and his son discuss a command, not a community's answer to messengers.
The jinn are urged to answer God's caller and believe, a direct positive formulation of the response at issue.
The Day of Decision is only general temporal background for the focus ayah.
The sending of stones for punishment is not an account of answering messengers.
Patience toward what opponents say gives only an indirect response-to-message context.
No punishment occurs until a messenger is sent, directly grounding why a people's response to messengers is judged.
The messenger is brought as a witness over his community, directly supporting the accountability implied by asking their answer.
Messengers are sent to be obeyed by God's permission, defining the response expected of their recipients.
Obeying the messenger is equated with obeying God, clarifying the gravity of the answer under review.
Messengers bring good news and warning so people have no argument before God, grounding the later interrogation.
The command to deliver the revealed message supplies the messenger side of the communication for which hearers are questioned.
God's questioning of Jesus about worship gives a close Day-of-judgment interrogation involving a messenger and his followers.
Jesus testifies that he commanded worship of God and then leaves knowledge of their later conduct to God.
Humans and jinn are asked whether messengers recited God's signs and warned them of this Day, directly matching the focus logic.
The arrival of messengers reciting signs sets the choice between reverent response and denial for every human community.
For every community a messenger comes, after which judgment is made with justice, closely framing 28:65's court scene.
Later messengers bring clear proofs but are denied, providing another concrete answer pattern.
Communities reject their messengers and demand proof despite clear signs, directly depicting refusal of the messenger's address.
A messenger is sent to every community with the call to worship God and avoid false gods, clarifying the content of accountability.
A witness is raised from every community and the Prophet is brought as witness, strongly parallel to the focus ayah's judgment setting.
People reject a messenger because he is human, supplying a specific objection that constitutes their answer.
Messengers are sent as bearers of good news and warners, explaining the function of the message to which an answer is due.
The hypothetical plea for a messenger before humiliation shows why prior messengership removes excuse at judgment.
Every messenger receives the same summons to worship God alone, identifying a shared message that communities either answer or refuse.
Successive messengers are called liars by their peoples, giving a repeated historical form of the answer assessed in the focus ayah.
The messenger's complaint that his people abandoned the Quran gives an explicit account of communal non-response.
God could have sent a warner to every town, reinforcing the relation between warning and communal responsibility.
People facing calamity wish a messenger had been sent so they could follow the signs, directly articulating the excuse precluded by 28:65.
God does not destroy towns before sending a messenger to recite His signs, providing the immediate surah principle of prior warning.
The messenger's duty is only clear conveyance, distinguishing delivery from the recipients' responsibility to respond.
Whenever a warner comes to a town, its affluent people reject the message, giving a social pattern of refusal.
No community lacks a warner, extending the universal scope of accountability for reception.
The people of the Fire admit that a warner came to them, an explicit retrospective acknowledgment of ignored warning.
People repeatedly mock messengers when they come, directly naming their recurrent answer to prophetic address.
The earth is illuminated, the record and prophets are brought, and judgment is given, closely framing the focus's eschatological inquiry.
The people entering Hell are asked whether messengers came reciting signs and warning them of this meeting, a direct parallel.
The keepers of Hell ask whether the messengers brought clear proofs, making the recipients' prior answer central to punishment.
Messengers come from before and behind commanding worship of God, while their people reject their humanity as messengers.
Messengers of resolve patiently convey warning; the reminder of a Day of meeting supports the focus ayah's final accounting.
Messengers are sent with clear proofs, scripture, and balance, establishing the public evidence behind later questioning.
The command to obey God and the messenger and the messenger's duty of clear conveyance jointly clarify reception and responsibility.
A severe punishment is prepared for those who oppose God's command, and the following messenger makes the warning context explicit.
The keepers of Hell ask its people whether no warner came to them, directly revisiting ignored messenger warning.
The condemned admit that a warner came but they denied him, an exact confession of their answer to the messenger.
Disobeying God and His messenger leads to Hell, stating the consequence of refusing the communicated call.
The appointment of messengers to a fixed time belongs to the same eschatological setting in which their reception is exposed.
